title: Predators and wildlife management shape local‐scale nutrient heterogeneity by altering carcass deposition rates
content:
Large-mammal carcasses provide large pulses of nutrients into landscapes, with important implications for local biodiversity. In this paper, Andrew Abraham et al. examine how predators and wildlife managers dynamically interact with large-herbivore population dynamics to determine the overall rate of carcasses. Together, these top-down forces can promote fine-scale heterogeneity and the biodiversity that thrive in these unique elemental niches.


Abstract

Large-mammal carcasses create spatially concentrated nutrient pulses that increase environmental heterogeneity and promote biodiversity. Both predators and humans can alter the rate of large-animal carcass availability through mortality events or offsite removal. However, it is not well understood how these processes interact with wildlife population dynamics to influence nutrient heterogeneity across scales. Here, we compiled data on the difference in concentration of nitrogen (N) and 15N-isotopes in plants growing on and off 201 large-mammal carcass sites as a proxy for how long nutrient signals persist after carcass deposition for different-sized animals. Our dataset was derived from four continents, spanned body masses 10–4000 kg and extended from 0 to 12 years after the carcass was deposited. We used Generalised Additive Mixed Models and integrated the resulting predictions of carcass-derived nutrient elevation and persistence into an agent-based model (ABM) that simulates the population turnover of large-herbivore species. Our empirical results reveal that both %N and δ15N signals in plants peaked after 2 years before declining to background levels within 4–8 years. While the absence of long-term measurements for the largest-bodied carcasses precluded us from assessing the expectation that elevated nutrient signals persisted for longer at these sites, our results confirm that the magnitude of the nutrient peak increases with body mass. ABM simulations revealed that predation and wildlife management interacted dynamically with ungulate density-dependent processes to determine carcass deposition rates. Maximum carcass deposition rates peaked at mid-levels of predation or culling and were lower at high mortality (due to lower ungulate density) and low mortality (due to slower population turnover). Carcass deposition rate and size were positively related to increased plant nutrient heterogeneity at the local scale but did not significantly alter plant heterogeneity at the landscape scale. Synthesis: Carcass-mediated nutrient heterogeneity emerges from the interaction between individual carcass characteristics and population-level mortality processes. Predators and wildlife management can therefore indirectly shape nutrient redistribution by altering both herbivore population dynamics and the rate at which carcasses enter ecosystems. Wildlife managers should engage with carcass deposition processes holistically to promote fine-scale nutrient heterogeneity and associated biodiversity.
